title: From Temporal Mindsets to the Finish Line: A Prospective Study of Time Perspectives and Trail-Running Performance.
abstract: Recent research has highlighted the role of time perspectives in distance running performance, supporting the core predictions of the conceptual model of time perspective in athletic functioning. We examined whether time perspectives predict trail-running performance in 227 participants of the Ultra Roztocze in Poland. The event featured five International Trail Running Association-certified distances, spanning submarathons (11.5-35.6 km) and ultramarathons (65.2-124.5 km). Performance was operationalized using Rate My Trail score, a time-based metric allowing cross-distance comparisons. We aimed to replicate prior findings, test their robustness while controlling for Big Five traits and body mass index, and examine race distance as a moderator. Future-positive consistently predicted better outcomes, whereas present-fatalistic was negatively associated with performance, even after accounting for personality and body mass index. The effects of present-hedonistic varied by distance. These findings demonstrate the incremental validity of time perspectives, highlighting temporal orientation as a valuable target for endurance athletes' psychological preparation.
